zh: 区间端点可达 10^18，不能逐个检查；但满足条件的数非常少：二进制最多 60 位，最高位必为 1，其余位里只能有 1 到 3 个 0。
可以把所有 beautiful 数直接枚举出来：对每个位长 b，从全 1 的数 2^b−1 中把 1 到 3 个非最高位改成 0。总数约五十万，排序后对立方和做前缀和，每个查询用二分回答。
先读入全部查询并求出最大的 R，只枚举不超过它的数：位长从 2 到 R 的二进制位数，在非最高位中选 1、2、3 个位置并减去对应的 2 的幂。排序后建立立方和对 998244353 取模的前缀数组（先取模再相乘，避免溢出）。对每个查询，用“第一个不小于 L 的位置”和“第一个大于 R 的位置”取前缀之差，调整为非负余数后输出。
en: Endpoints go up to 10^18, so checking numbers one by one is impossible; but qualifying numbers are rare: at most 60 binary digits, the top bit is 1, and only 1 to 3 of the other bits are 0.

So enumerate every beautiful number directly: for each bit length b, start from the all-ones number 2^b−1 and clear 1 to 3 of the bits below the top. That gives about half a million numbers; sort them, build prefix sums of cubes, and answer each query with binary search.

Read all queries first and take the largest R, enumerating only numbers up to it: for bit lengths from 2 to the bit length of R, choose 1, 2 or 3 positions below the top bit and subtract those powers of 2. After sorting, build a prefix array of cube sums modulo 998244353, reducing before multiplying to avoid overflow. For each query take the prefix difference between the first position not less than L and the first position greater than R, and print it as a non-negative residue.

explanationEn:
## Fixed source and correction of the wrong example

fastprep/Moveworks/moveworks-sum-of-cubes-of-beautiful-numbers.md at the fixed commit e66f809f4c953bce129f68491726176615db6afc states clearly: a positive integer is beautiful only if its binary representation, with leading zeros removed, contains at least 1 and at most 3 zeros. Each query asks for the sum of the cubes of all beautiful numbers in the closed interval [L,R], modulo 998244353. The full ranges 1≤Q≤200000 and 1≤L≤R≤10^18 are never reduced.

The original input [[5,8],[10,15]] is kept, but both the original output [153,0] and the explanation [637,0] are wrong. The qualifying numbers in [5,8] are 5(101), 6(110), and 8(1000), whose cubes sum to 125+216+512=853; in [10,15] they are 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, whose cubes sum to 9000. 15 is 1111, which has no 0, so it does not qualify. This site explicitly corrects the answer to [853,9000] rather than changing the definition to fit the wrong example. The other two public examples were derived by this site.

The raw starter and its return type say a single long, but the Input/Output section of the same source clearly specifies Q lines of intervals and Q integers of output. This problem follows that explicit multi-query output contract and prints the Q results one per line; a newline is one form of whitespace separation, and the queries are not arbitrarily aggregated into a single value. Leading zeros are not counted; 1 (1) does not qualify and 2 (10) does; 0 is not in the input domain. No upstream code was executed.

## Approach

Let a number's binary length be b. The highest bit must be 1; among the remaining b−1 bits, choose exactly 1, 2, or 3 positions to be 0, and all other positions are 1. Enumerating b and this set of positions and subtracting the corresponding powers of 2 from 2^b−1 gives every beautiful number. Keep only values not exceeding the largest R of the current input, sort them, and build a prefix array of cube sums modulo the modulus. Use two binary searches to find the left boundary for L and the right boundary for R, take the difference of the prefixes, and reduce it to a non-negative residue.

## Proof of correctness

The enumeration only changes 1s below the highest bit to 0, so the resulting number's actual bit length is indeed b, and its number of non-leading zeros is exactly the number of chosen positions, 1..3; after discarding values greater than the largest R, every kept number satisfies the definition. Conversely, every valid number has a unique bit length and a unique set of zero positions, so it is generated by the corresponding enumeration exactly once. Therefore the sorted array neither misses nor repeats any number a query may need.

Entry j of the prefix array is the sum of the cubes of the first j sorted numbers, modulo the modulus. lower_bound(L) gives the count of numbers less than L and upper_bound(R) gives the count not greater than R, and between them lie exactly all beautiful numbers in the closed interval [L,R]. The prefix difference is congruent to the true cube sum modulo the modulus, so taking the non-negative residue gives the unique correct answer.

## Complexity and full boundaries

10^18<2^60. The number of enumerated candidates is at most Σ(b=1..60)Σ(k=1..3)C(b−1,k)=C(60,2)+C(60,3)+C(60,4)=523625; after cutting the numbers above 10^18, exactly 491280 remain. With K candidates, the time is O(K log K+Q log K) and the space is O(K+Q); powers and cubes are computed on bounded integers, cubes can be reduced modulo the modulus first, and Python also supports full big integers. Nothing scans number by number up to 10^18.

An independent digit DP over the whole domain finds 491280 valid numbers, with a cube sum of 497027816 modulo the modulus. At the maximum Q=200000 the small-input limits cannot be applied: the formal data includes a full input of about 8000007 bytes and up to 200000 results, so this site uses the existing 32MiB input budget and a 2048KiB runtime output limit, and the complete package stays below 100MiB and the 128MiB import limit.

## Independent verification

The oracle neither enumerates zero-bit combinations nor uses the reference's sorted prefixes. It runs a digit DP over the binary bits from high to low, with states for whether it is tight against the upper bound, whether the first 1 has been seen, and the number of effective zeros, maintaining the sums of the 0th through 3rd moments of the values. Appending bit d turns x into 2x+d, and the moments are updated by binomial expansion; zeros before the start are not counted, and at the end only states that have started and have 1..3 zeros are taken. A query's result is F(R)−F(L−1). For small ranges, results are also cross-checked number by number, counting zeros with bin after removing leading zeros and summing cubes directly.

163 unique oracle cases pass against the real reference subprocess. The formal data includes a recomputation of the original wrong example, both endpoints, all ones / one zero / three zeros / four zeros, changes of binary length, values close to 10^18, the whole domain, and two sets of a full 200000 queries. Repeated endpoints use a cached digit DP; the many small intervals have their expected outputs generated separately from number-by-number brute-force prefixes, so the reference algorithm is never used as the oracle. The two negative controls wrongly include numbers with no zero and wrongly exclude the right endpoint, respectively; on all formal data they must exit normally before a kill is counted.
